To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of Guineans belong to West African‐specific sub‐clusters of the L0‐L4 mtDNA haplogroups, with the exception of a new L3 subcluster, L3h, which is also present in eastern Africa.
the majority of the mtDNAs of Guinean samples belong to West African sub‐clusters of haplogroups L0‐L4 and that a new sub‐cluster (haplogroup L3h) is found at moderately low frequencies.
the majority of the mtDNAs of Guineans belong to haplogroups that are specific to West African populations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a more detailed characterization of the mtDNA diversity of the Senegamba region.
the genetic composition of the Guinean populations and the genetic relationship of these populations with other West African and East African populations.
a better understanding of the genetic diversity in West Africa, and the role of the Senegambian corridor as a genetic bridge between West and East Africa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mtDNA line of evidence suggests that Guinean populations have been shaped by both the Bantu and the Berber migrations.
, in addition to the presence of Sudanese and Saharan‐related lineages in Guinean mtDNA, a substantial number of lineages are shared between West‐ and East‐African mtDNA pools.
the mtDNA line‐age distribution of the Guinean population is a mixture of sub‐Saharan, North‐African and Sudanese elements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in addition to the Sudanese origin of some of the Guinean ethnic groups, there was a significant input from the eastern and western African populations.

, in general, the Guinean populations have a genetic profile that reflects their geographical location in West Africa, but also that their matrilineal ancestry is more complex than previously thought.
the mtDNA composition of Guineans is a mixture of the ancient West African and more recent East African lineages.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Guinean populations are genetically homogeneous and that the majority of the mtDNAs found in Guineans belong to the West African specific subclusters of the L0‐L2 haplogroups, with the L3 sub‐clusters being found at lower frequencies.
the genetic diversity of the Guinean region is a result of the interplay of the three main genetic components of West Africa, the Mande, the Sudanese and the Berber.

Guinean mtDNA lineages are predominantly of West‐African origin and the presence of East‐African haplotypes in Guinean ethnic groups with a Sudanese origin may be the result of a recent admixture with the local populations.
